name: Hives (urticaria)
definition: Hives, also called urticaria or nettle rash, is an itchy, raised rash that can appear anywhere on the body.
overview: Hives is an itchy, raised rash that is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. It can appear as bumps or patches of different shapes and sizes, and it may itch, sting or burn. Swelling deeper under the skin, called angio-oedema, often occurs alongside it. Hives usually gets better within a few days, although it can come back.
causes: A reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals
Other triggers can include infections, medicines, cold, heat, sweating, scratching and tight clothing
Some cases have no identifiable cause
riskFactors: Exposure to a known trigger, such as a food, a medicine or an insect sting
signs: Raised bumps or patches on the skin in many shapes and sizes, anywhere on the body
Swelling deeper in the skin (angio-oedema), often of the lips, eyelids or mouth
complications: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, which needs a 999 call
Difficulty breathing, which can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) needing emergency treatment
Hives that last for six weeks or more, known as chronic urticaria
diagnosis: Hives is usually recognised from the appearance of the rash and the history, and routine allergy tests are not needed for most people with spontaneous urticaria who respond to antihistamines. Basic blood tests such as a full blood count may be used to rule out other conditions. For some physical types, a provocation test such as an ice cube test may be used.
treatment: Mild hives often clears within a few days and can often be treated at home, and a pharmacist can advise on antihistamines. If the rash does not clear, a GP may prescribe menthol cream, antihistamines or steroid tablets, and may refer the person to a dermatologist. For longer-lasting hives, first-line treatment is a non-sedating antihistamine, and the aim is to control symptoms until the condition settles. Omalizumab is reserved for severe cases and is available in specialist clinics.
prevention: Where a trigger is known, avoiding or reducing it is part of care. The BAD leaflet advises avoiding aspirin, ibuprofen and codeine unless essential, because these may aggravate urticaria.
seekCare: Call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is difficult, or if someone faints or cannot be woken. NHS 111 or a GP the same day is the route if the rash has not improved after 2 days, is spreading or keeps returning, or if there is a high temperature and the person feels unwell. Otherwise a GP appointment is the route for hives that continue.

sections.heading: What are hives and what do they look like?
sections.body:
Hives, or urticaria, is an itchy, raised rash that is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. The rash can appear as raised bumps or patches in many shapes and sizes, and it can show up anywhere on the body. It may itch, sting or burn.

Some people also have angio-oedema, which is swelling deeper under the skin. Swelling of the lips, eyelids or mouth is typical, and it is often painful rather than itchy. Most urticaria is not inherited. Hereditary angio-oedema is a separate condition that runs in families. Hives usually gets better within a few days. The NHS allergies page says hives can be a sign of allergy.

sections.heading: What triggers hives?
sections.body:
The NHS lists many possible triggers, including certain foods, contact with plants, animals or chemicals, cold, heat and sweating. Medicines, insect stings and infections can also set it off, as can scratching or tight clothing.

A UK primary care guide based on NICE CKS says acute urticaria may be caused by allergy to foods, drugs, irritants, insect bites and stings, physical stimuli and viral infection. Some cases have no identifiable cause. The BAD leaflet also describes inducible types, in which hives follow a specific stimulus such as cold, heat or friction. Another form, called cholinergic urticaria, is covered in the same leaflet. An NHS hospital trust leaflet links chronic urticaria to heat, cold, pressure or emotion in some people.

sections.heading: How long do hives last?
sections.body:
The BAD describes acute urticaria as an episode lasting up to six weeks. Chronic, or long-lasting, urticaria lasts for six weeks or more. In the NHS account, hives usually gets better within a few days.

Chronic urticaria is often spontaneous, which means that no specific trigger is found. In about half of the people with chronic spontaneous urticaria, the rash lasts for 6 to 12 months and then gradually disappears. It can last considerably longer, and the course in any one person is unpredictable. A rare cause is urticarial vasculitis, in which a very small percentage of people with an urticarial rash develop weals that last longer than 24 hours.

sections.heading: How are hives diagnosed?
sections.body:
The BAD says that diagnosis is usually based on the history and the look of the rash rather than on tests. Routine allergy tests are not necessary for most people with spontaneous urticaria who respond to antihistamines.

A UK guide based on NICE CKS says basic blood tests, such as a full blood count, may be used to rule out other conditions. For physical types, the same guide says a provocation test such as the ice cube test may be used to confirm the diagnosis. It also says that sun-related cases can be referred for ultraviolet light testing.

The same guide says the underlying cause should be identified and managed if possible.

sections.heading: How are hives treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says hives can often be treated at home and that a pharmacist can advise on antihistamines. If the rash does not clear, a GP may prescribe menthol cream, antihistamines or steroid tablets, and may refer the person to a dermatologist.

For longer-lasting hives, the BAD says the aim of treatment is to control symptoms until the condition settles, rather than to cure it. First-line treatment is a non-sedating antihistamine. A person and their doctor may need to try different antihistamines to find the one that suits best. A short course of steroid tablets may be given for severe urticaria. Omalizumab is kept for severe cases and is available only in specialist clinics. People who do not respond to antihistamines, or who are at risk of severe reactions, are referred for specialist review.

sections.heading: Living with hives and when to get help
sections.body:
The BAD leaflet advises avoiding aspirin, ibuprofen and codeine unless they are essential, because they may make urticaria worse. Where a trigger is known, avoiding or reducing it is part of care.

The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is difficult, or if someone faints or cannot be woken. It advises urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111 if the rash has not improved after 2 days, is spreading or keeps returning, or if there is a high temperature and the person feels unwell. For children, NHS Healthier Together advises contacting a GP if symptoms last longer than six weeks or are hard to control with regular antihistamines. Breathing problems with hives need urgent medical help.

faqs.a: The NHS says hives is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals. Other triggers include infections, medicines, cold, heat, sweating, scratching and tight clothing. Some cases have no identifiable cause, according to the BAD.

The NHS says hives usually gets better within a few days. The BAD describes acute urticaria as lasting up to six weeks and chronic urticaria as lasting six weeks or more. In about half of people with chronic spontaneous urticaria the rash clears within 6 to 12 months, but it can last longer.

The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is difficult, or if someone faints or cannot be woken. The BAD also says breathing problems need urgent medical help.

faqs.q: Are hives caused by an allergy?
faqs.a: They can be, but not always. The NHS says hives can be a reaction to things such as food, pollen or insect bites. The BAD says routine allergy tests are not necessary for most people with spontaneous urticaria who respond to antihistamines.

faqs.q: What is the difference between hives and angio-oedema?
faqs.a: Hives is a rash on the skin surface, while angio-oedema is swelling deeper under the skin. The BAD says angio-oedema often occurs with urticaria and typically affects the lips, eyelids or mouth.
